title: How Saturation Divers Eat, Shower & Sleep Under Pressure for 28 Days
asof: Figures as of 2026 · sources in description

shots.s: You're about to move into a steel tube on the deck of a ship.
Once the door seals, you can't come out.
Not for a day.
Not for a week.
For up to twenty-eight days.
Every day, you'll ride a metal bell to the bottom of the sea.
And the trip back home takes days.
So how do you eat,
shower,
and sleep,
under pressure?
The job is down there.
Pipelines and oil wells, sometimes a hundred meters deep or more.
At that depth, your body soaks up gas.
Coming up too fast could kill you.
So instead of coming up after every dive,
you just stay at depth pressure.
On deck, in a sealed chamber.
Your body fills up with gas once.
After that, a longer stay doesn't make the trip home longer.
That's saturation.
Most saturation diving happens between about sixty-five and a thousand feet.
You don't breathe normal air down here.
You breathe helium mixed with oxygen.
Helium is easy to breathe.
But it does strange things.
Your voice goes high and squeaky.
So high the crew outside can barely understand you.
They use a machine to unscramble it.
And helium steals your body heat,
with every breath you breathe out.
So the chamber is kept hot.
Often around ninety degrees Fahrenheit.
Your food is cooked in the ship's galley.
Then it's carried to the chamber.
It goes in through a tiny airlock.
The lock seals,
the pressure matches yours,
and you open the inner door.
Medicine, clean clothes and bedding come in the same way.
You eat at a little table,
inches from your bunk.
Your chamber has a shower.
And a toilet.
The waste is dumped outside the chamber.
Toilets have a valve lock.
It stops the dump from running while someone is sitting on it.
It's warm, damp, and shared.
That's perfect for germs.
In the 1970s,
two North Sea saturation dives were stopped by ear infections.

d.small: stopped by ear infections · North Sea, 1974–75

shots.s: So you keep your ears clean and dry.
Now, the work.
The bell locks onto the chamber.
You climb in.
The bell is lowered through a hole in the ship.
Down to the seabed.
You leave the bell,
tied to it by a hose called an umbilical.
It brings your gas, your light, and hot water for your suit.
A British rule sets the limits.
A whole bell run, no more than eight hours.
In the water, usually no more than four.
st: max in the water, two-man bell

shots.s: Then back up, back into the chamber.
Eat. Sleep. Repeat.
Things can go wrong.
In September 2012,
diver Chris Lemons was a hundred meters down in the North Sea.
His ship's positioning system failed.
The ship drifted away.
His umbilical snagged,
and snapped.
He had a few minutes of emergency gas on his back.
It took the ship about half an hour to get back.
They found him on the seabed, unconscious.
A colleague got him into the bell,
and gave him two breaths.
He came around.
He survived, and went back to diving.
So what if the ship catches fire?
You can't just jump overboard.
Your body is still at depth pressure.
So the chamber has its own lifeboat.
A pressurized one.
You climb into it, still under pressure.
It's sealed, and dropped into the sea.
Finally, it's time to go home.
But you can't just open the door.
The pressure comes down slowly.
One rule of thumb: a day for every hundred feet, plus a day.

d.small: per 100 ft of depth, plus 1 · DAN

shots.s: From a hundred and twenty meters, that's about five days.
You sit. You sleep. You wait.
And then, the door opens.
Your first breath of normal air in weeks.
And then the rules say: rest on land.
Usually as long as you were inside.
So, could you live in a steel tube for twenty-eight days?
Off Limits Life.

d.tag: How people live where you can't go
